records.text: The main task is to turn an autoencoder into a generative model.
A straightforward autoencoder maps each input point x to a single latent code z.
Sampling new points in the latent space of a straightforward autoencoder is difficult because the code space is not densely populated.
The core idea of the variational autoencoder (Kingma et al., 2013) is to let every input x map not to a single latent code but to an entire distribution q(z|x).
The decoder in a variational autoencoder must be stable to small changes in z.
The variational autoencoder can be seen as an improved version of a denoising autoencoder.
The variational autoencoder aims to cover the latent space with wide enough distributions.
If a variational autoencoder is trained without constraints, the encoder will prefer to decode from extremely narrow distributions and eventually collapse to a zero-variance distribution.
Therefore, a constraint (regularizer) must be added on q(z|x) to enforce that it stays close to a simple prior, e.g., a standard Gaussian.
The VAE aims to train an encoder q(z|x) that maps images x to latent codes z and a decoder p(x|z) that reconstructs images from z.
The joint distribution p(x,z) factorises as p(z)p(x|z) and as p(x)p(z|x).
p(x) is the complex, unknown distribution of images.
p(z) is a simple prior that can be sampled from, e.g., N(0,I).
p(z|x) is the encoder distribution.
p(x|z) is the decoder distribution.
To obtain a generative model, both p(x|z) and p(z|x) must be learned.
Because p(x) is very complex, one of the two distributions must be chosen to be simple and the other complex.
The VAE chooses to assume that p(z|x) is simple and p(x|z) is complex.
The VAE assumes p(x|z) = N(x | f(z), cI), where f(z) = Decoder(z).
The VAE assumes the prior p(z) = N(z | 0, I).
The VAE uses a variational approximation q(z) ≈ p(z|x) by parametrising the encoder with a Gaussian distribution q(z) and maximising a lower bound on the log-likelihood.
Starting from log p(x) = log p(x,z) - log p(z|x), taking expectation over q(z) yields E_q(z)[log p(x)] = E_q(z)[log p(x,z)] - E_q(z)[log p(z|x)].
By standard manipulations, log p(x) = E_q(z)[log p(x,z)] - E_q(z)[log q(z)] + E_q(z)[log q(z)] - E_q(z)[log p(z|x)].
This expression can be rewritten as log p(x) = ∫ q(z) log(p(x,z)/q(z)) dz + ∫ q(z) log(q(z)/p(z|x)) dz.
Thus, log p(x) = L(q) + KL(q(z) || p(z|x)), where the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is L(q) = ∫ q(z) log(p(x,z)/q(z)) dz.
Maximising L(q) with respect to q minimises the KL divergence, making q(z) a good approximation to p(z|x).
For the VAE, the ELBO becomes L(q) = ∫ q(z) log(p(z)p(x|z)/q(z)) dz = ∫ q(z) log p(x|z) dz + ∫ q(z) log(p(z)/q(z)) dz.
This simplifies to L(q) = ∫ q(z) log N(x | f(z), cI) dz - KL(q(z) || p(z)).
The VAE ELBO simplifies to L(q) = -1/(2c) E_q(z)[||x - f(z)||^2] - KL(q(z) || p(z)).
The first term in the VAE loss is the reconstruction loss, and the second term is a regulariser that pushes q(z) towards the prior p(z) = N(0,I).
When the encoder is Gaussian q(z|x) = N(z | μ_x, diag(σ^2_x)), the KL divergence has the closed form KL(q(z)||p(z)) = 1/2 ∑_{j=1}^d (σ^2_{x,j} + μ^2_{x,j} - log σ^2_{x,j} - 1).
Therefore, the final VAE loss function is L(q) = -1/(2c) E_q(z)[||x - f(z)||^2] - 1/2 ∑_{j=1}^d (σ^2_{x,j} + μ^2_{x,j} - log σ^2_{x,j} - 1).
To train the VAE, gradients must be backpropagated through the sampling of z, but direct sampling is not differentiable.
The reparametrization trick samples auxiliary noise u ~ N(0,I) and transforms it as z = μ_x + σ_x ⊙ u.
With the reparametrization trick, the randomness goes through u, allowing gradients to flow to the parameters μ_x and σ_x.
During training, for each mini-batch of images x, a matching mini-batch of u is sampled and used together with x.
Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) proposed training a Markov chain that gradually turns random noise into the desired data distribution, inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics.
In diffusion models, a forward chain progressively destroys the data by adding noise, and then we learn to reverse each step to generate samples from pure noise.
Let the data be x_0 distributed according to p(x_0).
The forward diffusion process adds Gaussian noise at each step t: q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = N(x_t | √(1-β_t) x_{t-1}, β_t I), where β_t is a noise schedule.
Over T steps, q(x_{1:T} | x_0) = ∏_{t=1}^T q(x_t | x_{t-1}).
Thanks to the reparametrization trick, x_t can be sampled directly in closed form.
With α_t = 1 - β_t and A_t = ∏_{i=1}^t α_i, and ε ~ N(0,I), x_t can be expressed as x_t = √A_t x_0 + √(1-A_t) ε.
Thus, the marginal distribution of x_t given x_0 is q(x_t | x_0) = N(x_t | √A_t x_0, (1-A_t)I).
If β_t is small, the reverse distributions q(x_{t-1} | x_t) are also Gaussian, but their parameters depend on the entire data distribution.
The reverse process is defined with learned parameters θ: p_θ(x_{0:T}) = p_θ(x_T) ∏_{t=1}^T p_θ(x_{t-1} | x_t), where each p_θ(x_{t-1} | x_t) = N(x_{t-1} | μ_θ(x_t,t), Σ_θ(x_t,t)).
If x_0 were known, the reverse step could be computed analytically.
Conditioning on x_0, q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) = q(x_t | x_{t-1}, x_0) q(x_{t-1} | x_0) / q(x_t | x_0).

Completing the square yields q(x_{t-1} | x_t, x_0) = N(x_{t-1} | μ̃(x_t,x_0), β̃_t I), where β̃_t = (1-A_{t-1})/(1-A_t) β_t and μ̃(x_t,x_0) = (√α_t (1-A_{t-1})/(1-A_t)) x_t + (√A_{t-1} β_t/(1-A_t)) x_0.
Using x_t = √A_t x_0 + √(1-A_t) ε_t, the mean simplifies to μ̃(x_t,x_0) = 1/√α_t (x_t - (1-α_t)/√(1-A_t) ε_t).
The training goal in diffusion models is to approximate the true reverse step without conditioning on x_0 by minimizing a variational bound.
Taking expectation over the forward process yields the loss function L = E_q(x_{0:T})[log (q(x_{1:T}|x_0)/p_θ(x_{0:T}))] ≥ -E_q(x_0)[log p_θ(x_0)].
Expanding the ratio gives L = E_q[-log p_θ(x_T) + ∑_{t=1}^T log(q(x_t|x_{t-1})/p_θ(x_{t-1}|x_t))].

After further manipulation, L decomposes into a sum L = L_T + L_{T-1} + ... + L_0, where L_T = KL(q(x_T|x_0) || p_θ(x_T)), L_t = KL(q(x_t|x_{t+1},x_0) || p_θ(x_t|x_{t+1})) for t=1,...,T-1, and L_0 = -log p_θ(x_0|x_1).
All L terms are KL divergences between Gaussians, which can be computed analytically.
For intermediate steps, the reverse model's mean μ_θ(x_t,t) is trained to approximate μ̃(x_t,x_0) = 1/√α_t (x_t - (1-α_t)/√(1-A_t) ε_t).
Since x_t is known during training, the noise can be parametrised directly: p_θ(x_{t-1}|x_t) = N(x_{t-1} | 1/√α_t (x_t - (1-α_t)/√(1-A_t) ε_θ(x_t,t)), Σ_θ(x_t,t)).
DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) refines the earlier diffusion framework with the same loss structure.
In DDPM, the forward diffusion variances β_t are fixed hyperparameters, so all q-distributions are untrained and L_T is a constant.
In DDPM, the variances in the reverse model p_θ(x_t|x_{t+1}) are also not trained, allowing a closed form for L_t.

For the final decoding step L_0, DDPM introduces a separate discrete decoder: for integer data in {0,...,255} rescaled to [-1,1], it models p_θ(x_0|x_1) = ∏_{i=1}^D ∫_{δ-(x_{0,i})}^{δ+(x_{0,i})} N(x | μ_{θ,i}(x_1), σ^2_1) dx, with integration limits extending 1/255 on each side.
At sampling time, DDPM can use the mean μ_θ(x_1) without noise.
DDPM achieved excellent generation quality, comparable to the best GANs of the time.
The earlier Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) results had only worked well on small datasets like CIFAR.
DDIM (Song et al., 2020) addresses the slow generation speed of prior diffusion models that require thousands of sequential steps.
Sampling from a trained GAN is about 1000× faster than from DDPM for the same image size.
The DDIM loss depends only on the marginals q(x_t|x_0), not on the full joint q(x_{1:T}|x_0), so a different forward joint with the same marginals can be used without changing the loss.
DDIM generalises to non-Markovian forward processes, provided a reverse Markov chain exists.
In DDIM, the forward process is defined implicitly via its reverse: q_σ(x_{1:T}|x_0) = q_σ(x_T|x_0) ∏_{t=2}^T q_σ(x_{t-1}|x_t, x_0).
The forward conditional in DDIM is obtained by Bayes’ theorem: q_σ(x_t|x_{t-1},x_0) = q_σ(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0) q_σ(x_t|x_0) / q_σ(x_{t-1}|x_0).
The marginals under DDIM remain unchanged, so the reverse diffusion can be trained with the same ELBO and yields a Markov chain.
By approximating the noise from x_0 to x_t, DDIM can take larger reverse jumps, achieving a 10×–100× speedup over DDPM without loss of quality.
Generation in DDIM can be made deterministic by setting the reverse variance to zero, making each latent code x_T correspond to exactly one image.
With deterministic generation, DDIM becomes a good model for latent representations, enabling smooth interpolations in the latent space.
DDPM could not produce smooth latent interpolations because of high noise.
Stable Diffusion (Rombach, Blattmann et al., 2022) trains a diffusion model on latent codes from a pretrained autoencoder, moving the diffusion into a lower-dimensional latent space.
This latent diffusion dramatically reduces computational cost while preserving high quality.
unCLIP (DALL‑E 2, Ramesh et al., 2022) factorises conditional image generation as p(x|y) = p(x|c,y) p(c|y).
In unCLIP, a prior model p(c|y) produces a CLIP embedding c from a text description y.
In unCLIP, the decoder p(x|c,y) first generates a noise (prior) for the image and then uses a diffusion model conditioned on c and y.
Midjourney is another diffusion‑based image generation model.
Diffusion Transformers (DiT, Peebles, Xie, 2022) is a latent diffusion model that replaces the U‑Net backbone with a transformer.
The input to the DiT model is an \(I \times I \times C\) tensor.
The input tensor is patchified into a sequence of \(p \times p\) patches.
The sequence length is \(T = (I/p)^2\).
The patch size \(p\) quadratically influences computational complexity.
The patch tokens are processed by DiT blocks.
DiT blocks use adaptive layer normalisation.
The normalisation parameters of the adaptive layer normalisation come from a conditioning signal (e.g., a time embedding).
Transformer GFLOPs correlate strongly with generation quality.
Large DiT models use computation more efficiently than U‑Net–based counterparts.
Flux is a later diffusion‑based model.
DDIM corresponds to a first‑order integration of an underlying ordinary differential equation (ODE).
Employing higher‑order ODE solvers (e.g., multistep second‑ or third‑order) can reduce the local error of the integration.
Employing higher‑order ODE solvers allows taking even larger steps during the reverse process.
As a result, even fewer reverse steps are required.
DPM‑Solver++ is more stable and efficient than previous approaches.
UniPC is a predictor‑corrector framework proposed by Zhao et al. (2023).
The UniPC framework includes a universal correcting step called UniC.
UniC can be added after any base predictor.
Adding UniC increases the order of accuracy without requiring additional model evaluations.
A matching predictor, UniP, is derived accordingly as part of UniPC.
Flow matching is the most significant recent direction in generative modeling.
Many modern generative models are based on flow matching.
Generative models are important.
Generative models are a great teaching tool.
Generative models demonstrate ideas that go through the whole of machine learning.
Variational approximation appears in its simplest and already useful form in variational autoencoders.
In an autoencoder, an input X passes through an encoder to produce a latent code Z.
The latent code Z is smaller than X.
A decoder attempts to reconstruct the original X, producing \hat{X}.
Training an autoencoder minimizes a reconstruction loss.
Examples of reconstruction loss for autoencoders are L2 norm and perceptual loss.
The reconstruction loss measures similarity between X and \hat{X}.
Autoencoders require no labels.
In autoencoder training, the dataset provides its own targets because the model reconstructs the same X.
The latent codes from an autoencoder live on a structured manifold within Z.
The manifold of latent codes does not cover the entire latent space Z.
If you sample a random point in Z, it will not fall on the manifold of plausible latent codes.
Therefore, the decoder will not produce a good image from a randomly sampled point in Z.
One approach to enable generative use of an autoencoder is the adversarial autoencoder.
In an adversarial autoencoder, a discriminator is added to distinguish real Z sampled from a target distribution (e.g., a Gaussian) from the encoder’s outputs.
The adversarial autoencoder applies the GAN idea to regularize the latent space.
The core idea of the variational autoencoder is to have the encoder output a whole distribution p(z|x) rather than a single point.
For a given input, the encoder outputs a Gaussian distribution in latent space.
A point is sampled from that distribution and used to reconstruct the same input.
By doing this for all training points, the resulting per-input distributions can overlap and cover the latent space.
This makes the latent space amenable to random sampling.
In practice, the VAE encoder outputs mean μ(x) and standard deviation σ(x) for a diagonal Gaussian.
The Gaussian is constructed from these parameters, then Z is sampled and passed to the decoder.
However, the encoder naturally tends to cheat: it can shrink the variance to zero, collapsing to a single point.
Alternatively, the encoder can push the means far apart to avoid overlap.
Both behaviors defeat the purpose of covering the latent space.
Therefore, a regularization term on μ and σ is needed to prevent σ from collapsing to zero and μ from diverging.
The regularization goal is to make the latent distribution similar to a standard normal distribution (mean zero, unit covariance matrix).
This regularization is the idea of the Variational Autoencoder.
Two problems arise in implementing the VAE: choosing the reconstruction loss and regularizer, and inserting a sampling operation into a deep neural network.
Choosing an appropriate reconstruction loss and regularizer is not trivial because there are many ways to measure closeness between distributions.
In the forward pass of a VAE, sampling from the Gaussian is straightforward, but gradients cannot flow through a sampling operation, so the backward pass breaks.
The formal approach to deriving the VAE loss considers two variables: x (the image) and z (the latent code).
Every machine learning model takes the joint distribution p(x,z) and decomposes it.
The joint distribution p(x,z) can be decomposed naturally as p(x,z) = p(x) p(z|x) or p(x,z) = p(z) p(x|z).
These decompositions correspond to the encoder and decoder components of a VAE.
p(z|x) is the encoder distribution produced by the encoder.
p(x|z) is the decoder distribution, which models a noise distribution around x, typically Gaussian.
p(x) is the true, highly complex global distribution of the data, which cannot be directly comprehended.
p(z) is the prior distribution on latent codes, needed to be a simple distribution for sampling.
To generate new data, we sample z from p(z) and then x from p(x|z).
If p(z) is a standard Gaussian and decoder noise is Gaussian, then p(z) p(x|z) is Gaussian.
But p(x) is extremely complicated (e.g., cat pictures), not Gaussian.
Therefore, both encoder and decoder cannot be assumed simple.
The more natural choice is to keep the decoder simple (Gaussian output noise).
This forces the true encoder distribution p(z|x) to be very complicated.
In a Variational Autoencoder, the complicated p(z|x) is approximated with a simple distribution q(z|x).
q(z|x) is a Gaussian whose parameters are output by the encoder network.
This approximation is a variational approximation.
Variational approximation is one of the most fundamental ideas in machine learning.
Starting from log P(X,Z), one can write log P(X) = log P(X,Z) - log P(Z|X).
Taking expectation with respect to an arbitrary distribution Q(Z) gives log P(X) = E_{Q(Z)}[log P(X,Z) - log P(Z|X)].
Adding and subtracting the entropy term E_{Q(Z)}[log Q(Z)] yields log P(X) = E_{Q(Z)}[log(P(X,Z)/Q(Z))] + E_{Q(Z)}[log(Q(Z)/P(Z|X))].
In the decomposition of log P(X), the second term is the Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(Q(Z) || P(Z|X)).
KL divergence measures how close Q(Z) is to the true posterior P(Z|X).
Therefore, log P(X) = L(Q) + KL(Q(Z) || P(Z|X)), where L(Q) is the first expectation.
Because log P(X) is constant with respect to Q, minimizing the KL divergence is equivalent to maximizing L(Q).
L(Q) is called the variational lower bound, or evidence lower bound (ELBO).
The ELBO L(Q) involves only the joint distribution P(X,Z), not the intractable posterior P(Z|X).
In typical models like the VAE, the joint distribution is simple (e.g., a product of Gaussians), making optimization feasible.
The variational approximation replaces a complicated, intractable distribution with a simpler one.
In practice, substituting specific distributions into the ELBO yields the VAE loss functions.
For the VAE, the ELBO expands to E_{Q(Z)}[log P(X|Z)] + E_{Q(Z)}[log P(Z)] - E_{Q(Z)}[log Q(Z)].
In the VAE ELBO expansion, combining the last two terms gives -E_{Q(Z)}[log(Q(Z)/P(Z))], which is the KL divergence between Q(Z) and P(Z).
In the VAE, Q(Z) is the approximate Gaussian with parameters μ_x and σ_x from the encoder.
P(Z) is the prior, typically a standard Gaussian.
Thus, the KL term enforces Q(Z) to be close to a standard Gaussian, serving as the regularizer.
The regularizer is an exact function of μ and σ derived from the KL divergence, implementable in PyTorch.
Without the variational approximation, one might not guess this regularizer; it emerges necessarily from the KL divergence.
An arbitrary regularizer (e.g., placing a gamma prior on σ) would be just a heuristic.
The first term of the ELBO, E_{Q(Z)}[log P(X|Z)], yields the reconstruction loss.
P(X|Z) is modeled as a Gaussian with mean from the decoder output and some noise variance.
Expanding log P(X|Z) (ignoring constants) gives a term proportional to -||X - decoder(Z)||^2.
Taking the expectation over Q(Z) yields the reconstruction loss.
In practice, the expectation is approximated by the empirical average over the training set.
Thus, the reconstruction loss becomes (1/n) Σ ||x_i - decoder(z_i)||^2, where z_i is from the encoder output for x_i.
The variational lower bound can be summarized as L = -const - c * L_recon - L_reg, where L_recon is MSE and L_reg is the KL regularizer.
Maximizing L is equivalent to minimizing the sum of reconstruction loss and regularizer with respect to encoder parameters that output μ and σ.
This derivation provides exact formulas, resolving the problem of choosing the loss function and regularizer.
The second problem is passing gradients through the sampling step.
The reparameterization trick solves this problem.
In the VAE pipeline, x goes to encoder to produce μ and σ, then z ~ N(μ, σ^2) is sampled, then z goes to decoder to produce \hat{x}.
The reparameterization trick restructures the network to allow gradient flow through the sampling step.
Sampling from N(μ, σ^2) is equivalent to sampling u ~ N(0, I) and setting z = μ + σ ⊙ u (component-wise multiplication).
In the reparameterization, u is sampled as an additional input independent of the encoder, making the subsequent transformation deterministic.
This allows gradients to flow from the loss back to μ and σ through z.
The reparameterization trick works for Gaussian distributions and some others, but not all distributions.
Training an autoencoder is relatively easy.
The high-dimensional data manifold is very complex.
Even the lower-dimensional latent space is non-trivial.
Sampling from a Gaussian in a low-dimensional space will not land on the latent manifold.
In a variational autoencoder, the encoder outputs entire distributions, not single points.
For each input, a distribution is placed in the latent space.
A point is sampled from that distribution, and the network must reconstruct the original input from any point in that distribution.
The goal is for these per-input distributions to cover the latent space, being wide enough and close together so that any sample from a standard Gaussian falls in a good region.
Without regularization, means will drift apart and variances shrink to zero.
Thus, a reconstruction loss and a regularizer for the encoder output are needed.
The variational approximation provides the exact reconstruction loss from the decoder model and the exact regularizer.
The reparameterization trick passes gradients through the sampling step by sampling from a standard Gaussian, multiplying by σ, adding μ, and feeding to the decoder.
VAEs did not catch on when they first appeared.
Early papers from about ten years ago used VAEs as a baseline that was not difficult to beat.
VAEs have been extended since their initial appearance.
A notable extension of VAEs is to discrete latent spaces.
In VAEs with discrete latent spaces, the latent variable $Z$ is a sequence of tokens.
Discrete latent spaces in VAEs enabled writing latent codes with a transformer from text, treating the process as machine translation.
DALL-E (2020/2021) used the approach of writing latent codes with a transformer from text.
By now, variational autoencoders underlie many modern generative models.
Diffusion models usually operate in a latent space, not pixel space.
It is too computationally expensive to perform diffusion directly on pixel space.
Diffusion models operate in the latent space of a modern variational autoencoder.
An example of a variational autoencoder used for diffusion is VQ-VAE.
VQ-VAE has a discrete latent space.
VQ-VAE adds adversarial losses to ensure local patch realism.
Modern diffusion models often operate in the latent space of VQ-VAE-like variational autoencoders.
Diffusion models, like VAEs, use a variational bound.
The foundational diffusion model paper was published in 2015 by Sohl-Dickstein et al., titled "Deep Unsupervised Learning Using Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamics."
The physics analogy in the diffusion model paper is based on a basic fact about Markov chains, not on statistical physics.
The forward diffusion chain adds noise to the input, gradually increasing the amount of noise.
After enough steps (hundreds of steps), the output of the forward chain becomes indistinguishable from randomness.
Starting with a crisp picture and repeatedly adding Gaussian noise, after about 500 steps the result is Gaussian noise indistinguishable from random sampling.
The goal of diffusion models is to reverse the noising chain into a denoising chain.
In the forward direction, the transformation is trivial (adding Gaussian noise).
The reverse direction requires a denoising procedure to remove Gaussian noise, which is much harder.
The reverse denoising cannot be done exactly unless the original image is known.
Conditional on the original image $x_0$, the reverse process can be performed exactly.
As a generative model, the goal is to start from random noise and gradually turn it into a realistic output.
The reverse chain can be approximated with a Gaussian, although the true reverse distribution is complicated.
The forward diffusion chain can be formalized by deriving closed-form formulas for moving multiple steps ahead.
The reverse process is formalized by deriving formulas for the reverse conditional on $x_0$, where exact denoising is possible.
A large variational approximation is made that jointly approximates every step in the reverse chain.
The reverse transformations are parametric, modeled by neural networks with parameters $\theta$.
At the start of the denoising chain, $p(X_n)$ is a simple standard Gaussian.
After the denoising chain, a sample from the target distribution (e.g., cat pictures) is obtained.
The approximation is performed by minimizing a loss function consisting of a sum of terms such as Kullback-Leibler divergences between Gaussians.
The loss is optimized via gradient descent to train the parameters of the reverse transition distributions.
The original diffusion model paper only worked for very small dimensions, such as CIFAR, and could not scale up.
For a while, diffusion models were forgotten.
Diffusion models were considered interesting but impractical because the reverse chain requires hundreds of steps.
The many steps correspond to hundreds of neural network evaluations to produce one image.
In 2020, DDPMs solved some technical problems of original diffusion models.
DDPMs achieved generation quality on par with the best GANs of that time, especially for faces.
DDPMs still performed poorly on diverse datasets like cats.
DDPMs did not solve the fundamental speed problem.
DDPMs still required hundreds of steps and were extremely slow.
Later in 2020, a different research group solved the speed problem.
The key idea was to switch from approximating the step from $x_{t+1}$ to $x_t$ to approximating the direction to the original $x_0$.
In DDIM, the reverse chain approximates the direction to the original $x_0$ rather than to the next point.
In DDPM, the reverse process goes step by step, requiring every intermediate point.
In DDIM, every step of the Markov chain approximates the direction straight toward $x_0$.
It is not possible to jump directly to $x_0$ in one step because the approximation is imperfect.
The DDIM approach allows taking much wider steps.
DDIM allows skipping steps.
Because each step aims toward $x_0$, you can move toward $x_0$ faster by taking longer strides.
DDIMs provided a 10 to 100 times speedup over original diffusion models without loss of quality.
DDIMs made diffusion models practical.
DDIMs were still slow and expensive.
The final step to modern diffusion models was performing diffusion in the latent space of an autoencoder rather than in pixel space.
The Stable Diffusion paper (2022) introduced latent space diffusion.
Stable Diffusion uses a diffusion process and a denoising architecture that operates on latent codes.
In Stable Diffusion, the denoising process starts from random noise $z_T$.
A conditioning signal, such as an encoded text prompt, is fed into each denoising step via self-attention or similar blocks.
After many denoising steps, the output latent code is decoded into an image by a variational autoencoder.
DALL-E 2 used a latent diffusion approach with pretrained CLIP embeddings.
CLIP embeddings provide a joint latent space for text and images.
In DALL-E 2, a decoder was trained to reconstruct images from CLIP representations.
In DALL-E 2, a diffusion model was trained inside the CLIP latent space to map text representations to image representations.
The images generated by DALL-E 2 were impressive for that time.
DiT replaced the internal denoising unit in latent diffusion with a full transformer.
DiT kept the same overall latent diffusion framework.
Flux is a direct successor of Stable Diffusion from the same team.
Flux further improved image quality.
Flux was a widely used open model.
Flux struggled with text rendering and complex prompt following.
Current state-of-the-art text-to-image models, such as GPT, Gemini, and Midjourney, are closed-source.
The exact architectures of these models are unknown.
It is almost certain that these models are latent diffusion models built on large autoencoders.
Generative models can be organized into explicit density models and implicit density models.
Among implicit density models, GANs remain relevant in niche applications.
Explicit density models include autoregressive models, such as WaveNet and LLMs that generate tokens one by one.
Explicit density models include flow-based models that gradually transform a simple distribution.
Explicit density models include approximate density models.
Approximate density models contain VAEs and diffusion models.
VAEs and diffusion models avoid strong assumptions about the true data distribution.
VAEs and diffusion models make assumptions about an approximation to the reverse process.
VAEs and diffusion models optimize via a variational bound.
VAEs approximate the posterior distribution $p(z \mid x)$.
Diffusion models approximate the reverse denoising chain.
All major generative models in the news are either autoregressive models or VAEs/diffusion models.
